Introduction
In recent decades, scientific advances have provided a deeper 
understanding of the energetic properties of living systems, 
beyond biochemistry, expanding the theoretical bases of biology 
and conventional medicine. Biophysics researchers have shown 
that the evolutionary process of living beings is governed by an 
omnipresent electromagnetic potential,1–3 which reinforces the 
concept of electromagnetic force as a product of one of the four 
known fundamental interactions. In mainstream medicine, biological 
systems are described from a biochemical perspective, where 
enzymes, proteins and other molecules interact in a seemingly chaotic 
manner within cells, performing vital functions through random 
collisions.4,5 However, this mechanistic view of a disorganized “soup” 
of biomolecules in suspension has been revisited, especially with the 
discovery of electromagnetic fields generated by cellular structures

Abstract
Silicon nanowires (Si NWs) are versatile one-dimensional building blocks for gas and biochemical sensors, MEMS/NEMS
physical transduction platforms, and integrated electronic devices because of their high surface-to-volume ratios and
compatibility with semiconductor processing. A key limitation of conventional top-down fabrication is its reliance on
furnace-based high-temperature steps, such as thermal oxidation and LPCVD, which can induce residual stress and
constrain post-CMOS integration because of thermal-budget limits above 400 °C. Here, we present a furnace-free, low-

underlying hard mask. After removal of the oxide layer,
the preform retains Cr sidewall protection while main-
taining top-surface coverage (Fig. 1g). The complete layer
removal is ensured through endpoint detection. Nomin-
ally, the recipes used are highly selective: the Cr removal
recipe yields a 65–70 nm/min etch rate, and the SiO2
removal recipe yields roughly 50 nm/min, with no mea-
surable SiO2/Cr removal under the applied conditions.
Release of the suspended NW is achieved using Bosch-
type DRIE with alternating etch (SF6/O2) and passivation
(C4F8) cycles. The isotropic etch component generates the
undercut required to release the structure from the bot-
tom surface, forming the suspended Si NW geometry
(Fig. 1h). DRIE is performed at the chip level using a
carrier wafer, with the platen set to ~1 °C. Etching is
performed with 5 s of etch and 2 s of passivation cycles to
achieve a release depth of 2 µm.

Nevertheless, excessive surface charge or uncontrolled

biomarkers will therefore be essential.
Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) 
may further accelerate the rational design of g-C₃N₄-
based nanoplatforms [138]. AI-assisted approaches could 
integrate synthesis parameters, structural descriptors, 
optical properties, catalytic activity, ROS profiles, cellular 
responses, and toxicity data to identify relationships that 
are difficult to derive from conventional trial-and-error 
approaches. Predictive models may facilitate optimiza­
tion of dopant concentration, defect density, heterojunc­
tion composition, particle size, and surface chemistry. 
However, the usefulness of AI models will depend on the 
quality, standardization, and comparability of the under­
lying experimental datasets. Establishing interoperable 
datasets and standardized characterization and biologi­
cal-assessment protocols will therefore be an important 
prerequisite for reliable AI-guided nanomaterial design.

Abstract
As the foundation of contemporary AI systems, the semi-
conductor industry is increasingly shaped by critical so-
cial, environmental, and geopolitical challenges. Nonethe-
less, prior research has often examined these issues in iso-
lation and within disciplinary silos, leaving a gap in under-
standing them through an integrative socio-technical, cross-

dential, and inconsistent (Kuo, Kuo, and Chen 2022; Ruberti
2023; Bui 2024). Several researchers argue that transparency
is crucial for understanding the complex materials, compo-
nents, and the impacts of resources beyond energy, such as
water and minerals, as well as emissions and manufactur-
ing processes involved in semiconductor production, espe-
cially given the global dispersion of the different steps of the
supply chain (Bui 2024; Pasricha and Wolf 2024; Ghulam
and Abushammala 2023). Further, placing a strong empha-
sis on transparency also enables collaboration among vari-
ous stakeholders within the supply chain (Bui 2024).
Some large IT companies, such as Apple, Amazon, Meta,
Microsoft, and Google, publicly disclose their carbon emis-
sions (Pasricha and Wolf 2024; Gupta et al. 2021; Google
2026; Apple Inc. 2025). Such disclosures are largely vol-
untary and self-scoped, with firms determining their own
boundaries and accounting conventions. They have accord-

4.4
The Knowledge Divide and Global Inequality
The workshop surfaced deep anxieties about the weaponiza-
tion of access to knowledge. Participants noted that cur-
rent competitive challenges are not just about market share,
but about structural exclusion. High capital expenditures
(CAPEX) and export restrictions effectively lock the Global
South and smaller nations out of the AI ecosystem, fueling
an innovational and educational knowledge gap that rein-
forces power imbalances and the “monopoly by design”. Si-
multaneously, labor risks are displaced to regions with com-
petitors emerging in other areas that may have weaker labor
protections, creating a race to the bottom.
This exclusion raises important questions about equity
and participation in the AI ecosystem: if certain regions can-

cal competitiveness, almost always considering them within
separate disciplinary silos. Our findings emphasize the im-
portance of inclusive, multi-stakeholder dialogue in shap-
ing the governance structures of this deeply infrastructural-
technological domain. Participants stressed the urgency of
addressing transparency gaps, knowledge asymmetries, and
the unequal distribution of both the benefits and burdens of
semiconductor production across the globe.
Beyond documenting these challenges, this paper makes
a broader claim about what AI ethics needs to pay atten-
tion to. AI ethics has largely confined its attention to the
software layer: model behavior, dataset practices, and algo-
rithmic outputs. Yet, we argue that semiconductors and the
hardware layer are not only the physical foundation of AI
systems; they are also a foundational layer of AI ethics. The
ethical implications of AI systems are not only instantiated
in the training data selected or the outputs deployed; they are
